back: An ordered rectangular array of numbers or functions. Elements/entries are the numbers or functions.

front: What is the order of a matrix?
back: A matrix with m rows and n columns is of order m × n.
When number of rows = number of columns (m = n), order n × n.
Column matrix: only one column (m × 1). Row matrix: only one row (1 × n).
A square matrix where all non-diagonal elements are zero: a_ij = 0 for i != j.
A diagonal matrix with equal diagonal elements: a_ii = k, a_ij = 0 for i != j.
A scalar matrix with k=1. a_ii = 1, a_ij = 0 for i != j. Denoted I_n or I.
A matrix in which all elements are zero. Denoted O.
Same order and corresponding elements equal: A=[a_ij], B=[b_ij], A=B iff a_ij = b_ij for all i,j.
If A=[a_ij], B=[b_ij] same order m×n, A+B = [a_ij + b_ij]_{m×n}.
kA = k[a_ij] = [k a_ij] for every element.
Commutative: A+B=B+A. Associative: (A+B)+C=A+(B+C). Identity: A+O=A. Inverse: A+(-A)=O.
A is m×n, B is n×p => AB is defined and is m×p (columns of A = rows of B).
No. AB != BA in general even if both are defined.

front: Can AB = O with A!=O, B!=O?
back: Yes, matrix multiplication has zero divisors (unlike real numbers).
(AB)C = A(BC) (associative). A(B+C)=AB+AC, (A+B)C=AC+BC (distributive). AI=IA=A.
Interchange rows and columns of A: if A=[a_ij]_{m×n}, A'=[a_ji]_{n×m}.
(A')'=A, (kA)'=kA', (A+B)'=A'+B', (AB)' = B'A' (reversal law).
A square matrix A is symmetric if A' = A, i.e. a_ji = a_ij.
A square matrix A is skew symmetric if A' = -A, i.e. a_ji = -a_ij. All diagonal elements are zero.

front: Decomposition into symmetric and skew symmetric
back: For any square matrix A, A = (A+A')/2 + (A-A')/2, where (A+A')/2 is symmetric and (A-A')/2 is skew symmetric.
A square matrix A is invertible if there exists B with AB = BA = I. B is A^{-1}.
Yes. If A is invertible, its inverse is unique.
(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1} (reversal law).
For any square matrix A, AI = IA = A where I is identity matrix of same order.
